subject: Nariway Daily Check-in - 2026-08-21
html:
Nariway Daily Check-in
21 August 2026
 
Needs your attention / action today

Delete one sentence in the report — a two-minute fix, open a fourth straight QA audit. Line 68 of the manuscript still says wealth-manager art-service adoption has “roughly doubled since 2011,” the exact causal reading the claims register forbids (the real 2023→2025 trend reversed, 63%→51%). The correct framing already sits two lines below it — just copy it up.

Decide what “the conversation model is settled” actually means. Substack Notes were paused 8/17 until “3 to 5 conversations prove the spine,” with no resumption trigger named. That count is 5 as of today (Hall Rockefeller and Adam Szymanski published; Sage Gee, Matthew Erskine, and Leslie Anderson confirmed), plus Kelly Cahn accepted for early September. Both the CFO and CMO stewards flagged this exact gap two days ago and it hasn’t moved since — worth naming on purpose before the count answers it by accident.
 
Today I learned

Heinz Berggruen sold his Picasso-and-Klee collection to the German state in 2000 for roughly a tenth of its market value, on purpose, so it would stay in Germany and in one building — then his family kept funding the museum for decades after giving up ownership entirely. In 2021, fourteen years after his death, his son Nicolas (still a board member) committed the family to €1M a year starting 2025, on top of full state funding. It’s a shape this dataset hasn’t coded before: a family staying on as funder with no ownership or control left to protect. Source note: cases/museum-berggruen.
 
What changed, and what it means

The outreach converted for the first time, instead of just going out. Sage Gee became the first-ever confirmed Conversation. Query B, live since 8/20, filled both of the two thinnest warm-network gaps with real people in the same day — Matthew Erskine (T&E attorney, questions already sent) and Leslie Anderson (museum leadership, drafting answers) — and Kelly Cahn (art advisor) accepted for early September. Asher Rubinstein passed gracefully on timing but the relationship stayed warm for a later wave. This is the first day the pipeline produced the referral channel itself, not just interest in being interviewed — still $0 earned, but the top of the funnel finally has real names in the seats that matter commercially.

The flagship report was repositioned this week, by Alina and an external review: the research is now the product, not a report you publish and move past. The new model is continuous research feeding a proprietary knowledge base, an annual report, and an escalating public conversation that culminates in launch — gated on one honest test, whether it produces real client situations, not article count. Nothing to do today; worth knowing the frame has shifted under the report you’ve been watching grow.

The case dataset grew from 62 to 68, alongside the first deliberate attempt to disconfirm H2 (“the receiving end is closing”). It narrowed rather than broke: museums do accept intact collections, but mainly from donors already structurally embedded as trustees, board chairs, or long-term loan partners — a real refinement of the report's central claim, not a reversal.
 
Where we stand

Still $0 earned, and H7B (will anyone pay) is exactly as unproven as yesterday. But today is the first time the outreach itself produced real people in the referral seats that matter, not just reach on the conversation series — that is a genuinely different kind of evidence than the case dataset or the report, even though none of it is revenue yet. The gap the CFO keeps naming is real: a well-built top of funnel, still no defined step from “conversation happens” to “bounded offer priced.”
